So last night a few friends of mine and I got into a debate with some cops. Don't worry, nothing bad happened; it was a calm pleasant debate and in my area police tend to be reasonable and actually behave like human beings, which means you can talk to them like actual human beings when given the chance.

Anyway, my friends and I were talking with a few cops about drug legalization and its merits. We were pro-legalization, they were against. One cop brought up an argument that has been puzzling me because it's one I've heard before. He argued, "The way I look at it, you have a choice." And he argued that people can always choose to buckle down and quit whatever drug they're on cold turkey, therefore they bear all of the responsibility of doing so and the state doesn't have any responsibility to help them, and every right to arrest them if they're caught.

I've heard this argument to justify police action and the actions of the legal system before, and it always confused, upset and befuddled me. The argument goes that everyone has a choice, all the time, no exceptions; that no matter what your circumstances you therefore always have a choice to break the law or not; therefore (this is the implied conclusion) the moral responsibility is always on the individual to follow the law regardless of circumstance, their ability to follow it, arguments that can be used in trial to justify one's actions including self-defense, etc.

To me this argument is nothing more than mental gymnastics police and lawyers use to place all of the moral responsibility for their actions on the ones doing it, and to absolve themselves of any wrongdoing. It always bothered me because it seems like cookie-cutter reasoning to justify going after anyone for any reason without having to actually look at the situation and serve justice rather than their own interests. It completely removes any moral responsibility or notion of choice from the police or the lawyers that use it -- by their own logic, don't they have a choice too, even more so than the individuals they're dealing with since they have guns and the power of the state behind them? Don't they have responsibility as authority figures to look at the facts instead of doing what they want and using others' actions to justify it? It seems so wrong, yet the argument appears so cogent and impenetrable that it scares me. After all, people do have agency and a choice, don't they? A domestic violence victim can choose to allow themselves to be emotionally or physically abused, or to simply run away and be homeless incurring all the risks in doing so, as opposed to fighting back which the cops would use as reasons to arrest them instead of their abuser. A homeless person can choose to starve, or just ask people for food/money incurring the risk that they might not be given it, or try to go to shelters and be turned away. Even if someone put a gun to your head and ordered you to commit a crime or be shot, you can always choose to be killed and be martyred; point in fact that's what many of our historical figures have done to bring about social change or to stand up to injustice. So therefore you're still choosing to break the law even though circumstances clearly dictate otherwise, therefore it's OK for the legal system to come after you, correct?

What makes this argument even more bizarre to me is that it implies that the police, lawyers, the state itself has no agency at all and just mindlessly reacts to whatever you're doing even though that's clearly not the case. My friends and I were having this discussion with the cops inside of a convenience store, actually, and during the discussion a homeless man walked in and shoplifted stuff. The police followed the man outside, searched him for what he stole, took it back and instead of arresting him, which is what their argument would conclude would happen, they chose to let him off with a warning. So how can they argue that everyone else has agency and therefore bears responsibility to capitulate to the state regardless of circumstance, but they have no agency and therefore aren't responsible for what they do to people when they just demonstrated that they clearly do have and exercise choice?

So I turn to you guys in considering the matter. The "you have a choice" argument seems so wrong but I can't quite articulate why. Can any of you, who are undoubtedly a lot better at parsing logic than I am, examine their (and my) argument and tear it apart, or perhaps offer your insight and experiences with that sort of thing?

At least in the case of drug use, I think it's a perfectly reasonable argument to say that the drug user lost their freedom of choice once they became physically addicted to the substance. A slightly more tenuous argument would be to bring psychological addiction into the fold, although I personally think this should be included. Either way, there's a certain point at which I don't think it's right to say "they could just quit cold turkey ". For example, a heroin addict might do things they really don't want to do- like stealing money from their close relations or pawning a family heirloom. But they do it because they have to feed the beast or they will get sick.

If they truly had a choice, would they do these things that hurt people close to them and further their isolation? Maybe if they're a dick, but I think it's more complicated than that. Some drug users get to a point in which they need help in order to quit. It's easy to say "they could quit if they wanted to" when you have no idea what it's like to have your thoughts and wishes under the influence of an addiction, but it just isn't that simple. The best thing we could be doing with drug users is to give them the option of rehab instead of prison. That's how we give them back their freedom of choice- by helping them develop the tools to start making their own choices again.

I dunno, this whole argument belies a lot of right-wing thinking, particularly against the poor, that it is their responsibility to help themselves therefore no one including the state should help them. The US justice system is really good at the punishment side if things but not as good at turning criminals into law abiding, productive members of society. Bannerman Castle - Pollepel Island, New York

Francis Bannerman purchased Pollepel Island in November 1900, for use as a storage facility for his growing surplus business. Because his storeroom in New York City was not large enough to provide a safe location to store thirty million surplus munitions cartridges, in the spring of 1901 he began to build an arsenal on Pollepel. Bannerman designed the buildings himself and let the constructors interpret the designs on their own. Most of the building was devoted to the stores of army surplus but Bannerman built another castle in a smaller scale on top of the island near the main structure as a residence, often using items from his surplus collection for decorative touches. The castle, clearly visible from the shore of the river, served as a giant advertisement for his business. On the side of the castle facing the western bank of the Hudson, Bannerman cast the legend "Bannerman's Island Arsenal" into the wall.

Construction ceased at Bannerman's death in 1918. In August 1920, 200 tons of shells and powder exploded in an ancillary structure, destroying a portion of the complex. Bannerman's sales of military weapons to civilians declined during the early 20th century as a result of state and federal legislation. After the sinking of the ferryboat Pollepel, which had served the island, in a storm in 1950, the Arsenal and island were essentially left vacant. The island and buildings were bought by New York State in 1967, after the old military merchandise had been removed, and tours of the island were given in 1968. However, on August 8, 1969, fire devastated the Arsenal, and the roofs and floors were destroyed. The island was placed off-limits to the public.

Do you have any tips for people looking to start their career at Microsoft? :)

https://careers.microsoft.com would be a good starting point, sure, but I'd love to know more about the recruitment process from someone who experienced it.
Tips for a career at Microsoft?

What would you like to know? I can say a few things in general but if you have specific questions let me know:

  • We tend to hire people who have technical expertise, passion, and focus. Almost all Microsoft employees have some sort of side passion other than work, and they almost always are obsessive about their passions.
  • If you're new to the work force you're best looking for work as a co-op or joining the MACH program which specializes in hiring top talent directly out of university
  • If you're already in the work force you'll need to have experience and accomplishments related to the job you're applying for. Don't expect to make a career move and join Microsoft in one step.
  • It's very rare to join Microsoft at a higher level than you were at in a previous job. A lateral move is more common, and a slight move downward is the norm. If you were a director elsewhere expect to be a manager at Microsoft.
  • As with any job, knowing someone on the inside is a huge plus. That said, I was a cold hire (knew nobody, responded to an ad) so it's possible to join without connections, but it helps immensely.

I do a lot of interviewing, so if you have any questions about that process I'm happy to help. Note however that I'm not based in Redmond and every division is unique, so just because I say something doesn't make it a universal truth. :)
